notes.title: iOS 27 Review: AI Finally Takes Over The iPhone
notes.summary: BGR full review (Sept 11, 2026, days before the Sept 14 public release) of iOS 27 based on months of testing on an iPhone 17 Pro Max across multiple countries. Calls the new Gemini-powered Siri AI 'incredibly useful' -- 9/10 success rate finding specific messages/documents/podcast links from personal context, conversational multi-step Q&A, on-the-fly translation, proactive schedule rearranging -- and Apple Intelligence broadly 'one of the best applications of AI on the market' with upgraded Genmoji, Image Playground, Writing Tools, and photo editing (Clean Up, Expand, Spatial Reframing). Explicitly frames Apple as a late follower: 'it's also somewhat odd to be celebrating the efforts of a trillion-dollar company that is only now catching up with the demand for AI... Apple took its sweet time getting here... I just wish Apple had done so sooner,' and credits the improvement directly to Google Gemini underpinning the new Siri. Notes the new Siri AI features are excluded for users with a European Apple Account (regulatory carve-out) and require iPhone 15 Pro or newer plus a waitlist join. Otherwise iOS 27 is called 'fundamentally a minor upgrade' outside AI -- no major new features for Apple Music, most apps unchanged, single-tap password updates still not ready -- focused on Liquid Glass polish, bug fixes, and speed on older devices.

# iOS 27 Review: AI Finally Takes Over The iPhone
By [José Adorno](https://www.bgr.com/author/jose-adorno/) Sept. 11, 2026 4:00 pm EST
José Adorno/BGR
Add BGR on Google:
Preferred Source [Google Discover](https://profile.google.com/@bgr)
With the Release Candidate version of iOS 27 rolling out [just after the iPhone Duo event](https://www.bgr.com/2254151/apple-iphone-duo-foldable-price-release-date-specs/), we're now just days away from Apple [officially releasing iOS 27 to the public on Monday, September 14](https://www.bgr.com/2254215/ios-27-release-date/). With the foldable iPhone Duo now official and the new iPhone 18 Pro models finally revealed, we now have a clearer picture of the true capabilities of this upcoming software update.
Over the past few months, we've been using iOS 27 on an iPhone 17 Pro Max, putting this update to the test all over the world — from mainland China and Paris to Budapest and Berlin. Not only have we noticed [significant improvements since the first beta](https://www.bgr.com/2187533/how-to-download-ios-27-beta-guide/), but also how the new features and changes will reinvigorate Apple's smartphone lineup. While the iPhone 15 Pro and newer models will be acquiring powerful new Siri AI features, Apple says that older models will get snappier with tons of bug fixes, improved AirDrop reliability, and apps opening faster than ever.
After months of testing, we've learned about how the new features improve the iPhone experience, how the update impacts battery life, and who should be updating to this software once it becomes available for the iPhone 11 and beyond. Here's everything you need to know about iOS 27, Apple's biggest leap into AI so far.
## Liquid Glass has reached its final form
José Adorno/BGR
Visually, iOS 27 looks similar to iOS 26, but it's far more polished. Some apps have improved contrast and look more vivid. Even the Clear option for Liquid Glass, which on iOS 26 was washed out and hard to see with some backgrounds, has evolved. The entire iOS 26 update cycle seemed to focus on fixes and changes for Liquid Glass, but it took until the arrival of iOS 27 to bring the new design language up to the company's typical standards.
Liquid Glass has been Apple's push into a more unified design language across its operating systems, and, unlike during the Steve Jobs era, the company is willing to make compromises to appease users. For example, users can decide whether they want a glassy, translucent experience or a tinted look closer to iOS 18. In general, refraction is more uniform across the OS with the latest update. It's also important to note that the company requires iOS 27 apps to be easily resized to any format of display, which we now know was an effort to maximize compatibility with the foldable iPhone Duo.
iOS 27 not only looks beautiful, but owners of older iPhones should notice apps opening faster. With the modern powerhouse that is the iPhone 17 Pro Max, it's impossible to say that Instagram, iMessage, and other apps were suddenly opening dramatically faster, as the experience remains consistent with what was already present in iOS 26.
## Siri AI is incredibly useful
José Adorno/BGR
Apple's long-delayed promise of Apple Intelligence is finally a reality — even if it's still in beta. Rolling out to users globally in iOS 27 – except for those with a European Apple Account – the new Siri AI seems to be everything the company envisioned and, perhaps, a little bit more. It's such an enormous leap forward from Siri having a hard time setting a timer, sharing a weather report, or [knowing what month it is](https://www.bgr.com/tech/forget-apple-intelligence-siri-doesnt-even-know-what-month-it-is/).
The truth is, Siri AI is incredibly useful, and it's yet another push for the company's own services. The personal assistant shines when it's accessing Messages, Notes, Mail, and other first-party Apple apps. Nine out of 10 times, Siri was able to help me find a very specific message, document, podcast link, or even something I didn't fully remember. The personal assistant is conversational, gives me insights about my travel, can answer nearly any question, and translates on the fly. I've ever used it to figure out exactly how early I should wake up to eat breakfast before leaving a hotel for the airport.
Of course, Siri is not always perfect, and it sometimes forgets it can use Google. For example, if I ask for translation of an unsupported language like Hungarian, the personal assistant quickly tells me it's incapable of doing that. However, all it takes is reminding Siri it can browse the internet to find the translation online. Other features that have impressed me include asking Siri to replace a phrase with translated copy, adding information to a form, and proactively making my day easier by rearranging my schedule to avoid conflicts.
## Apple Intelligence has reached a new level
José Adorno/BGR
Every Apple Intelligence feature has been upgraded. Genmoji creation, for example is very proactive as you send messages — even though Apple will suggest some bizarre images. Image generation is also faster on Image Playground, Writing Tools is a constant reminder you might not know how to construct a phrase properly, and the AI-powered image editing tools impressed me the same way Pixelmator did years ago with how it used the iPad's machine learning capabilities to remove objects from photos.
iOS 27 features an improved Clean Up tool, which is much better at removing unwanted objects and people in the background of your photos. The Expand tool is great for adding to your photo to fill out the frame, and it also works surprisingly well. Finally, the ability to use Spatial Reframing, which lets you tweak the angle of a photo, almost makes me question if we should have so much added control over our shots.
While there's plenty worth being excited about, and anyone with an iPhone 15 Pro or newer model is going to have a wealth of new features to explore — [after they join the wait list for the new AI features, anyway](https://www.bgr.com/2214236/how-to-get-siri-ai-ios-27-public-beta-guide/) – it's also somewhat odd to be celebrating the efforts of a trillion-dollar company that is only now catching up with the demand for AI. Even though I'd consider Apple Intelligence one of the best applications of AI on the market, Apple took its sweet time getting here. That said, [there's no shame in asking Google for help](https://www.bgr.com/2073701/apple-next-gen-siri-powered-google-gemini/) — I just wish Apple had done so sooner.
## General improvements and battery life
José Adorno/BGR
Besides the full adoption of AI, iOS 27 is fundamentally a minor upgrade. There are no notable new features for Apple Music, most of Apple's apps look the same, and highly-anticipated additions, like the ability to update passwords with a single tap, aren't ready yet. Rather, Apple decided to deliver an update focused on fixing bugs, polishing up the code, and making the experience feel snappier.
For an iPhone 17 Pro Max user, it's honestly hard to tell the difference between iOS 26 and iOS 27. After all, every beta release introduces new bugs, though, with the iOS 27 Release Candidate now installed on my device, I can say that the software feels as stable as ever. For owners of an iPhone 12 or an iPhone 13, their devices should feel even faster than they did on iOS 26.
Of course, battery life is always a major concern when updates arrive. I've been charging my iPhone twice a day throughout the summer, which is due to a mix of Parisian heatwaves, testing every Siri AI feature, and a seemingly dry vapor chamber (that's not really how it works, but my iPhone 17 Pro Max does feel warmer around the camera plateau). However, for those who haven't been using the iOS 27 beta, Apple has been doing something clever: [indexing Siri and its apps for the iOS 27 release](https://www.bgr.com/2224284/ios-26-6-update-now-available-new-features/). What this means is that, the iOS 26.6 update already did most of the hard work, so iOS 27 should run even better than usual on day one. For me, every weekly update means a new round of indexing.
## Should you upgrade to iOS 27?
José Adorno/BGR
iOS 27 is a welcome upgrade for any iPhone owner — even those without the latest models and those who aren't interested in upgrading to an iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo. While an iPhone 11 owner might not find many new features in iOS 27, they will gain a more reliable AirDrop, faster speeds, and some battery improvements. For those with an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, the highlight is Apple Intelligence, which truly transforms the iPhone experience.
I personally really enjoy how the new Siri lives on the Dynamic Island and how notifications sit right next to the clock. That said, iPhone users will need to retrain their brains a bit, as the upper-right corner is dedicated to the Control Center, the upper-left corner is for notifications, and everything else around the top of the display is Siri AI and Spotlight.
Overall, I've been satisfied with iOS 27, and I'm looking forward to see what the new cycle of updates will bring. iOS 27.1 is still a mystery for now — it could add even more AI features or just make small tweaks. We've also put together [a checklist to prepare your iPhone for iOS 27](https://www.bgr.com/2245924/how-to-prepare-iphone-for-ios-27-update/), which is worth reading before the launch on September 14. Overall, this is one of the most polished software updates Apple has delivered in recent years.
## Recommended

notes.title: We Tried The New Siri Beta - Has Apple Finally Delivered On Its Promises?
notes.summary: SlashGear hands-on review (written during the iOS 27 developer beta, pre-final-release) of the long-delayed 'personal context' Siri first promised at WWDC 2024, testing on iPhone/iPad. Verdict: the new Siri (built on Google Gemini) is 'effectively on par with the original 2024 demo' -- successfully surfacing personal data across Messages, Photos, Notes, purchase history, and reading history via natural, vague queries, and offering strong on-screen awareness (act on visible content across any app, e.g. auto-filling forms, screenshotting and sending, setting reminders from on-screen context). Reports substantive rollout friction: (1) initial personal-context indexing took over a week on iPad and multiple days on iPhone even with modest ~200GB of data; (2) despite being pitched 'on-device first,' complex requests still route through Apple's Private Cloud Compute and fail/stall without good connectivity, meaning true offline use does not work as implied; (3) usefulness scales with how deep a user is in Apple's own app ecosystem (iMessage, Apple Mail, Apple Notes) versus third-party apps like Gmail/WhatsApp, though App Intents/MCP adoption could close this gap over time. Notes Apple paid 50 million to settle claims from users who bought iPhones expecting the 2024-promised Siri that was then delayed roughly two years.

# We Tried The New Siri Beta - Has Apple Finally Delivered On Its Promises?
By [Jordan Wirth](https://www.slashgear.com/author/jordanwirth/) June 30, 2026 4:30 pm EST
Cheng Xin/Getty Images
Add SlashGear on Google:
Preferred Source [Google Discover](https://profile.google.com/@slashgear)
Two years. Count 'em, it's been two years since [Apple Intelligence was unveiled in 2024](https://www.slashgear.com/1642396/apple-intelligence-best-features-iphone/) for iOS 18. The showstopper feature Apple presented at the time was a much-needed Siri upgrade boasting chatbot smarts paired with deep personal contextual awareness. That Siri was delayed. Repeatedly. Things got so bad that Apple coughed up $250 million to disgruntled users who bought iPhones for the new Siri, and rumors swirled that the entire demo had been a Silicon Valley fever dream. At long, long last, though, we have 2024's Siri via the OS 27 Developer Beta. Is it the princess that was promised?
I've been running the [iOS and iPadOS 27 Developer Beta](https://www.slashgear.com/2190962/how-to-download-ios-27-beta-iphone/) since it first released, and ever since I got off the Siri waitlist and both devices finished indexing, I've been throwing everything I could think of at Siri. Complex, unusual questions reminiscent of WWDC 2024's demo (and WWDC 2026's demo) to see whether Apple finally stuck the landing.
Please bear in mind this is all based on early OS 27 beta software, not the final product, so there were plenty of non sequitur answers, misunderstandings, and bugs. I am writing this with the assumption that by the time the full public release happens in September, Apple will have fixed most or all of the issues that I experienced. Here's how it went.
## Two years late, but worth the wait
Jordan Wirth/SlashGear
I won't leave you in further suspense: Yes, this new Siri is effectively on par with the original 2024 demo. Gone are the days of it completely misunderstanding basic requests, or hitting you with a "here's what I found on Google." It's a back-and-forth chatbot experience no different from Gemini or Claude, providing sources you can verify. Personal context is what sets it apart from the competition. WWDC 2024 showed a Siri that knows you intimately via your iCloud account content, and can surface emails, conversations, notes, photos, and more to serve as a helpful digital assistant.
Let me give some examples. I asked it what my Japanese homework was and it translated the conversation with my tutor to figure it out; it guessed when I had purchased a specific model of keyboard by recognizing it in my photos; it told me when and for how much I had sold a device online; when asked whether or not I had been to the place that inspired the "Spirited Away" movie, it pulled up my pictures from my Taiwan trip; it told me which book in the "Saxon Stories" series came next, knowing the ones I had read so far; when asked about my article on [switching to Mac from Windows](https://www.slashgear.com/1630218/switching-from-windows-to-mac-is-it-worth-it/), it summed up my conclusion. I could give examples all day, but the point is, the new Siri works as advertised.
To be abundantly clear, there were plenty of misfires. But when it works (and it does more than it doesn't), it works exceptionally well. I rarely had to baby it; I asked the questions above as vaguely as possible, and Siri often figured out from my personal context what I meant without follow-up clarification. For early beta software, this is incredibly promising.
## Indexing may take an eternity
Jordan Wirth/SlashGear
In order to understand your personal context enough to help you, Siri requires indexing. You'll see this when you open the Settings app on your device. Indexing is essential to get useful answers, so if you use Siri before the indexing is complete, your experience will be subpar. The problem is indexing — at least during the beta — can take an annoyingly long time to complete.
Since I was running the beta on both iOS and iPadOS, I tried two different approaches. On the iPad, I just used it normally; I charged the device when it was low and then just left it there when not in use. As a result, indexing took _forever._ Literally over a week. On my iPhone, I left it plugged in for hours at a time, and it finished in a couple of days. It's likely Apple will figure out how to make indexing go faster when OS 27 officially releases, but I can't imagine it'll take less than a couple of days for most people unless you leave your phone plugged in all night.
I should mention here that I don't have a huge amount of content on my devices and in iCloud, either. Maybe 200GB total for photos, iCloud Drive, notes, etc. So if someone has a much larger pool of personal content, I worry the indexing will keep them waiting for even longer before they can really use Siri. Here's to hoping it's not like that [common problem on iOS 26](https://www.slashgear.com/2054227/ios-26-common-problems-fixes/) where the reindexing after every update makes your phone get hot and zaps its battery — except this time, it temporarily kneecaps Siri for a few days.
## Siri may be on-device first, but you'll still need internet
Jordan Wirth/SlashGear
When I finally got off the Siri waitlist, I just happened to be away from home in a place with terrible Wi-Fi and cell signal. "Not a problem," I thought. "The new Siri is all on-device, so I should be able to use it comfortably with local data." Boy, was I wrong. Simple requests like setting reminders worked. Anything more complex than that — even if Siri had the info right there in front of its face — failed. This is because, I learned, even though the processing _does_ happen on device, Siri relies on Apple's Private Cloud Compute servers to know how to approach a request. My complex requests either took forever or failed until I found [a good Wi-Fi network](https://www.slashgear.com/1910787/things-in-home-negatively-affecting-disrupting-wifi-connection/).
In my view, Apple would do well to make this abundantly clear upon the official release. People are going to misunderstand the "on-device" part to mean that they could, in theory, go off the grid with their iPhone and have a fully functional digital assistant, which they won't. And of course, nobody's thrilled about these very personal requests being slingshotted into the cloud where they can only hope and pray that their data privacy won't be abused. None of this is helped by the fact that the new Siri is built on Google's Gemini.
Look, I get it. Most of us are connected to Wi-Fi and/or cellular virtually 24/7 with few exceptions. Just be prepared for Siri's new spinning thinking dots to take longer if you're on bad Wi-Fi.
## The deeper you're in the Apple ecosystem, the better (for now)
Runrun2/Shutterstock
The more thoroughly integrated your life is into Apple's services and apps — Photos, iMessage, Calendar, Contacts, Notes, Reminders, Music, Podcasts, etc. — the more useful and effective OS 27's Siri will be for you ... which could also be one of its biggest downsides. People who use, say, the Gmail app for email, WhatsApp for friend and family chats, and Microsoft OneDrive for files may come away disappointed if Siri can't talk to or source data from their preferred non-Apple apps.
I experienced this myself to an extent during my testing. Most of my chats are not in iMessage, so any questions leveraging previous conversations with family and friends fell on deaf ears. This was frustrating even though I have the lion's share of my personal data in Apple's ecosystem. I can't imagine how much more frustrating this will be for someone who uses even fewer Apple services — or none.
Having said that, this may just be an early beta limitation. Apps that incorporate App Intents and MCP (frameworks that basically make it easier for Siri to request data from third-party apps) could potentially make it irrelevant which apps you use. After the OS 26 release, it took time for apps to adopt Apple's Liquid Glass design language, but eventually most of them did. Give OS 27 a year or so to mature and I'd bet all the major apps will have already jumped on the App Intents bandwagon, making Siri capable for all users.
## On-screen awareness is the killer feature
Jordan Wirth/SlashGear
Everything I've mentioned so far is cool, but what's going to really be a game changer is on-screen awareness. At any time, in any app, you can summon Siri and ask it questions about what you see on screen, and have Siri act on your behalf. During the original WWDC 2024, the demo showed the presenter's Siri grabbing a driver's license number from a picture and inserting it into a form seamlessly with one request. You can do that now with this Siri, and so much more.
For example, I asked Siri to send the note I was viewing as a PDF to an email address; I asked it to screenshot the current page I was looking at and send it to one of my contacts; with Safari open, I asked it to open a new tab and show me the iPad Pro product page; in Google News, I asked it to identify the person in one of the headline images, and it did so; I asked it to "set a reminder for this" when on the PlayStation page for "Grand Theft Auto 6," and it did so; while looking at a picture of a receipt, it was able to copy all the text to a note. And a lot more.
I know these are random examples that may not necessarily be useful, but they demonstrate an incredible amount of potential beyond Apple's iffy recommendations during WWDC 2026 to make themed recipes for parties. As long as there's clear information on the screen, Siri can seemingly perform any basic action on it, and that's going to save you a lot of time with tedious tasks that you might have otherwise done manually.
## Recommended

# Apple CEO John Ternus says the best AI device is still the iPhone
10:36 AM PDT · September 9, 2026
Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, used the opening of the company’s [Surprise and Shine event](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/09/everything-apple-announced-at-its-fall-iphone-event-from-the-foldable-iphone-duo-to-an-always-listening-apple-watch/) Wednesday to make its AI strategy clear: The iPhone is already the best AI device out there, and Apple cares more about data privacy than its rivals.
The comments come as Ternus takes the reins at Apple from Tim Cook, who is now executive chairman, and offer a clear picture of how the company plans to compete in the AI era. Instead of building new hardware for AI, Apple wants to make the iPhone the central way consumers interact with the new technology.
During his introduction at the Cupertino event, Ternus described the ideal AI device as an “intelligent personal hub.” He said such a hub would have a broad understanding of a user’s personal context, always be with them, and have both a powerful processor capable of running AI models on-device and an internet connection to access models in the cloud.
The device would also have a large display, high-quality cameras, and microphones so it could see and hear the world around it, along with long battery life, Ternus continued.
Plus, “you’d want it to be super easy to use without a big learning curve. And finally, you’d want it to work seamlessly with your other devices, apps, and services, so it feels like one integrated experience,” he said.
“In other words, you would arrive at something remarkably familiar, because there’s no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone,” Ternus said. 
Ternus also emphasized how Apple cares more about data privacy, adding that “others see [users’ personal] data as something to collect and store.” It was one of the sharper statements Apple has made about how it intends to differentiate its AI platform from the competition.
“Honestly, trust only goes so far when your data is no longer yours to control; that’s why Apple Intelligence runs on device whenever it can,” Ternus concluded.

notes.title: Apple’s new CEO is reviving a Steve Jobs strategy from 25 years ago | TechCrunch
notes.summary: TechCrunch analysis of new Apple CEO John Ternus's first keynote (Sept 9, 2026, 'Surprise and Shine' event): Ternus explicitly recommits to the iPhone as Apple's AI-era hub, stating 'There's no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone,' and framing the ideal AI hub as needing 'a powerful processor, high-resolution cameras, persistent networking, and on-device AI.' Article frames this as a reversal of Tim Cook's push to diversify Apple beyond the iPhone, drawing an explicit parallel to Steve Jobs's 2001 'digital hub' Macworld keynote defending the Mac just before the iPod launch. Cites bearish pre-event press (Fortune, Axios) questioning the smartphone's future and Apple's post-Cook AI direction. No dedicated standalone AI device or Siri strategy is announced — the strategic bet is doubling down on iPhone-centric on-device AI rather than a new hardware form factor.

# Apple’s new CEO is reviving a Steve Jobs strategy from 25 years ago
1:58 PM PDT · September 9, 2026
Apple CEO John Ternus wants you to know that the iPhone isn’t going anywhere.
Ternus threw his weight behind the venerable device on Wednesday during his first keynote as CEO, placing it firmly at the center of Apple’s product strategy for the AI era. 
“There’s no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone,” he said. 
This contrasts with the approach taken by former CEO Tim Cook, who tried time and again to convince Wall Street that Apple was more than just the iPhone.
Ternus’ pitch is also a rebuttal to pundits who have recently cast doubt on the iPhone. “The smartphone’s days are numbered,” said [one headline](https://fortune.com/2026/05/18/smartphones-days-numbered-ai-wearable-devices/). “The Tim Cook era is coming to a close with an existential challenge for Apple: figuring out what comes after the iPhone,” said [another article](https://www.axios.com/2026/04/21/apple-tim-cook-iphone-ai).
But it’s not just about the hardware. Ternus has put the iPhone at the center of his [“intelligent personal assistant” strategy](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/09/apple-ceo-john-ternus-says-the-best-ai-device-is-still-the-iphone/), a vision that could define the company for years to come. Steve Jobs did something similar in 2001 with the Mac, less than 10 months before he announced the iPod.
At the time, many observers thought the PC’s days were numbered. At a Macworld New York keynote, Jobs called out bearish quotes from industry wonks like Walt Mossberg and the leaders of Compaq and Gateway. 
“This is what everyone else is telling us. That our PC is waning if not the hole being dug,” Jobs said at the time, pointing at a tombstone for the “Beloved PC” on the screen behind him. “We don’t think the PC is dying at all. We don’t think the PC is moving away from the center at all. We think it’s evolving, just like it has since it was invented.”
“We think the PC is on the threshold of entering its third great age,” Jobs added, a prediction driven by the proliferation of digital devices at the time, including camcorders, digital cameras, and DVD players. 
The Mac would form the center of a “digital hub” that would connect these disparate devices and, in Jobs’ words, “add value” to all of them.
Later that year, Jobs pulled the iPod out of his pocket, a device seemingly developed to answer the question, “Why do you still need a PC?” The device turned out to be an enormous hit, driving Apple’s profits quarter after quarter and ultimately helping lead to the development of the iPhone.
Today, with the iPhone on the cusp of its 20th anniversary, Ternus is facing a version of the same question Jobs took on in 2001. We don’t know if Ternus is quietly sitting on an iPod-like product, one that will secure the iPhone’s position as Apple’s hub for years to come. But he is firmly rebutting the idea that the iPhone is past its prime.
“If you were designing the ideal version of this hub from scratch, how would you do it?” Ternus asked before listing the ingredients: a powerful processor, high-resolution cameras, persistent networking, and on-device AI.
It helps that the iPhone is [one of the most powerful](https://www.macworld.com/article/2455063/the-first-a18-pro-benchmarks-are-out-and-it-is-fast.html) personal computing devices around, giving it an edge in the compute-hungry AI era. Its portability and adaptability make it, for many people, the only computing device they need. Even among those who own laptops and iPads, the iPhone is often the one device they can’t live without. Plenty of people leave home without their laptops. Almost no one leaves without their phones.
That combination of power and portability has given Apple a privileged position in the AI world. Other companies have attempted to unseat the iPhone with all manner of wearable devices, but none have succeeded.
Instead of sidelining the iPhone in favor of the next flashy thing, Ternus is leaning into it instead. In a way, he’s bringing Apple around to what the rest of us already know: The iPhone is pretty great, and maybe we don’t need to replace it with something else. Yet.
